meta.titre: Wave phenomena: reflection, refraction, diffraction and interference
meta.sous_theme: behaviour of waves at boundaries, gaps and overlaps

sections.contenu_markdown: When someone calls your name from behind a wall at school in Bertoua you still hear them clearly even though you cannot see them, when you shout in a valley in the Adamawa plateau your voice comes back a moment later, and when two loudspeakers play the same note in a hall some seats seem much louder than others. These everyday experiences are reflection, diffraction and interference. At the GCE you must name the phenomenon, say what changes and what stays the same, and complete a simple calculation or a sketch of wave fronts.

items: Wave speed, frequency and wavelength are linked by $v=f\lambda$.
A wave front is a line joining points on a wave that are in step, such as the crests of ripples.
Sound travels at about $330\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ in air.

sections.titre: Reflection, refraction, diffraction and interference of waves
sections.contenu_markdown:
**Reflection.** A wave bounces off a barrier. The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, both measured from the normal. The speed, frequency and wavelength do not change. Examples: an echo, a ripple bouncing off the side of a tank, the image in a mirror.

**Refraction.** A wave changes **speed** when it passes from one medium to another (or from deep to shallow water), so its direction changes if it meets the boundary at an angle. The frequency stays the same because it is fixed by the source, so by $v=f\lambda$ the wavelength changes in the same proportion as the speed. Water waves moving from deep to shallow water slow down, the wavelength shortens and the waves bend **towards** the normal.

**Diffraction.** Waves spread out when they pass through a gap or round the edge of an obstacle. The spreading is greatest when the **gap width is about the same size as the wavelength** (or smaller); with a very wide gap the waves go straight through with only slight spreading at the edges. Speed, frequency and wavelength **do not change**. This is why you hear sound (wavelength about $0.5\ \mathrm{m}$) round a corner more easily than you see light (wavelength about $5\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{m}$).

**Interference.** When two waves meet, the resultant displacement is the sum of the individual displacements (superposition). If two waves arrive **in phase** (crest meets crest), they add and the amplitude is large: **constructive interference**. If they arrive **out of phase** (crest meets trough) they cancel: **destructive interference**.

| Phenomenon | Speed | Frequency | Wavelength | Direction |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Reflection | same | same | same | changes (angle $i=r$) |
| Refraction | changes | same | changes | changes at an angle |
| Diffraction | same | same | same | spreads out |

variantes.nom: Wave fronts in a ripple tank
variantes.quand_utiliser: When asked to describe or sketch what happens to wave fronts at a barrier, a gap or a boundary.
variantes.contenu_markdown: **Barrier:** straight wave fronts reflect as straight wave fronts at equal angles to the barrier. **Narrow gap (about one wavelength):** the straight wave fronts become **circular arcs** spreading out beyond the gap. **Wide gap:** the wave fronts continue straight in the middle with a small curving at each edge. **Deep to shallow:** the wave fronts stay parallel to each other but come closer together (shorter wavelength) and change direction if they meet the boundary at an angle.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When two loudspeakers or two ripple dippers produce loud and quiet places or large and small ripples.
variantes.contenu_markdown: At points where the waves from the two sources arrive in phase, the resultant amplitude is $A_1+A_2$ (loud sound, large ripples). Where they arrive out of phase, it is $|A_1-A_2|$, which is zero if the amplitudes are equal (silence, flat water). Interference needs the two waves to have the same frequency and a steady phase relationship (coherent sources). Energy is not destroyed at the quiet places; it is redistributed to the loud places.

sections.enonce_markdown:
In a ripple tank, straight water waves of frequency $10\ \mathrm{Hz}$ and wavelength $3.0\ \mathrm{cm}$ travel in deep water. They pass into a shallow region where their speed falls to $20\ \mathrm{cm\,s^{-1}}$.

(a) Calculate the speed of the waves in deep water.

(b) Find the frequency and the wavelength in the shallow water.

(c) The waves in deep water then go through a gap in a barrier which is $3.0\ \mathrm{cm}$ wide. Name and describe what happens to the wave fronts.

etapes.justification: Speed is the product of frequency and wavelength.

etapes.action: State the frequency in shallow water.
etapes.justification: The frequency is set by the source and does not change at the boundary.
The wavelength is shorter where the speed is lower, so the wave fronts are closer together.

etapes.action: Name the effect at the gap.
etapes.justification: The gap width ($3.0\ \mathrm{cm}$) is about the same as the wavelength.
etapes.resultat_markdown: This is **diffraction**: the wave fronts spread out as circular arcs beyond the gap, with the same wavelength and frequency.

sections.conclusion_markdown: **(a)** $30\ \mathrm{cm\,s^{-1}}$. **(b)** $f=10\ \mathrm{Hz}$ (unchanged) and $\lambda=2.0\ \mathrm{cm}$. **(c)** Diffraction: circular wave fronts spread out beyond the gap.

items.erreur_markdown: “When a wave goes into shallow water its frequency decreases.”
items.pourquoi_faux: The frequency is fixed by the source of the wave. Only the speed and the wavelength change.
items.correction_markdown: In refraction the frequency is constant; $v$ and $\lambda$ decrease together because $v=f\lambda$.

items.erreur_markdown: “Diffraction makes the wavelength longer as the waves spread out.”
items.pourquoi_faux: Waves spread out without any change of speed, frequency or wavelength. Only their direction of travel is affected.
items.correction_markdown: Diffracted waves have exactly the same wavelength and frequency as the incident waves.

items.erreur_markdown: “Destructive interference destroys the energy of the waves.”
items.pourquoi_faux: Energy is conserved. The waves cancel at some places but the energy is found at the places of constructive interference.
items.correction_markdown: Destructive interference gives zero (or very small) amplitude at certain points; the energy is redistributed.

items.erreur_markdown: Two waves of amplitude $6\ \mathrm{cm}$ interfere constructively, so the amplitude is “the average, $6\ \mathrm{cm}$”.
items.pourquoi_faux: Superposition means the displacements are added, not averaged.
items.correction_markdown: The resultant amplitude is $6+6=12\ \mathrm{cm}$ (and $0$ for perfectly destructive interference).

items.enonce_markdown:
Name the wave phenomenon in each situation: reflection, refraction, diffraction or interference.

(a) A girl hears her friend speaking round the corner of a building.

(b) A shout in a valley is heard again about a second later.

(c) Two loudspeakers playing the same note produce loud and quiet places in a room.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) **Diffraction**: the sound spreads round the corner.

(b) **Reflection**: the sound is reflected by the hillside (an echo).

(c) **Interference**: the two sets of sound waves add in some places (loud) and cancel in others (quiet).

items.enonce_markdown: A boy stands in front of a high wall and claps his hands once. He hears the echo $0.40\ \mathrm{s}$ after the clap. Take the speed of sound in air as $330\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. Calculate the distance between the boy and the wall.
items.solution_markdown:
The sound travels to the wall and back, so the total distance is $330\times0.40=132\ \mathrm{m}$.

Distance to the wall $=\dfrac{132}{2}=$ **$66\ \mathrm{m}$**.

items.enonce_markdown:
A sound of frequency $660\ \mathrm{Hz}$ travels in air at $330\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ towards a doorway $0.90\ \mathrm{m}$ wide. Light of wavelength about $5\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{m}$ also reaches the doorway.

(a) Calculate the wavelength of the sound.

(b) Explain why a person standing beside the doorway, out of the straight line, can hear the sound but cannot see the source.

(c) Two waves of amplitudes $5\ \mathrm{cm}$ and $3\ \mathrm{cm}$ meet at a point. Find the largest and smallest possible resultant amplitude.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) $\lambda=\dfrac{v}{f}=\dfrac{330}{660}=$ **$0.50\ \mathrm{m}$**.

(b) The doorway ($0.90\ \mathrm{m}$) is of the same order as the wavelength of the sound ($0.50\ \mathrm{m}$), so the sound is **diffracted** strongly and spreads into the room beside the doorway. The wavelength of light is about $1.8\times10^{6}$ times smaller than the doorway width, so light is hardly diffracted and travels in straight lines; the person cannot see the source from the side.

(c) Largest (constructive): $5+3=$ **$8\ \mathrm{cm}$**. Smallest (destructive): $5-3=$ **$2\ \mathrm{cm}$**.

items_markdown: Reflection: angle of incidence = angle of reflection; speed, frequency and wavelength unchanged (echoes).
Refraction: speed and wavelength change, frequency stays the same ($v=f\lambda$); waves bend towards the normal when they slow down.
Diffraction: waves spread through a gap or round an obstacle, most when the gap is about one wavelength wide; speed, frequency and wavelength are unchanged.
Interference: displacements add. In phase gives constructive interference ($A_1+A_2$); out of phase gives destructive interference ($|A_1-A_2|$).
Name the phenomenon first, then say what changes (if anything) and what stays the same.
